blocks.body:
How large can $|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|$ get as $t\to\infty$? To the right of the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=1$ the zeta function is bounded; to the left of $\mathrm{Re}\,s=0$ the functional equation makes it grow like a power of $|t|$. The critical line sits in between, and the size of $\zeta$ there governs moments, zero counts and primes in short intervals.

In 1908 Ernst Lindelöf conjectured that on the critical line $\zeta$ grows more slowly than any power of $t$. This is still open. What can be proved for free is the exponent $\tfrac14$; every improvement on it is called a subconvexity bound, and the same name is used for the analogous problem for every $L$-function.

blocks.title: The Lindelöf function and the Lindelöf hypothesis
blocks.body:
For real $\sigma$ let
$$\mu(\sigma)=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R:\ \zeta(\sigma+it)\ll|t|^{a}\ \text{as }|t|\to\infty\}.$$
The Lindelöf hypothesis (LH) is the statement $\mu(\tfrac12)=0$, that is,
$$\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll_\varepsilon|t|^{\varepsilon}\qquad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.$$
So $\mu(\sigma)$ is the growth exponent of $\zeta$ on the vertical line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=\sigma$, and LH says that on the critical line there is no power growth at all.

blocks.title: What is known for free
blocks.body:
For $\sigma>1$, $|\zeta(\sigma+it)|\le\zeta(\sigma)$, so $\mu(\sigma)=0$. On the line $\sigma=1$ one has $\zeta(1+it)\ll\log|t|$, so $\mu(1)=0$ as well.

The [[functional-equation|functional equation]] $\zeta(s)=\chi(s)\zeta(1-s)$, with
$$\chi(s)=2^{s}\pi^{s-1}\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi s}{2}\Bigr)\Gamma(1-s),$$
transfers information from the right to the left. Stirling's formula gives
$$|\chi(\sigma+it)|=\Bigl(\frac{|t|}{2\pi}\Bigr)^{1/2-\sigma}\bigl(1+O(1/|t|)\bigr)$$
uniformly for $\sigma$ in a bounded interval. In particular $|\chi(\tfrac12+it)|=1$ exactly (this follows from $\chi(s)\chi(1-s)=1$ and $\overline{\chi(s)}=\chi(\bar s)$), and taking growth exponents in the functional equation gives
$$\mu(\sigma)=\tfrac12-\sigma+\mu(1-\sigma).$$
For $\sigma\le0$ this yields $\mu(\sigma)=\tfrac12-\sigma$ exactly. So we know $\mu$ on both sides of the critical strip; the whole problem is the strip $0<\sigma<1$.

blocks.title: Convexity bound
blocks.body:
The function $\mu$ is convex, continuous and non-increasing on $\mathbb R$, and
$$\mu(\sigma)\le\frac{1-\sigma}{2}\quad(0\le\sigma\le1),\qquad\text{in particular}\qquad\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll_\varepsilon|t|^{1/4+\varepsilon}.$$

blocks.title: Proof of the convexity bound
blocks.body:
The tool is the Phragmén–Lindelöf principle, a maximum principle for vertical strips: if $f$ is holomorphic on $a\le\mathrm{Re}\,s\le b$, satisfies a crude growth bound such as $|f(s)|\ll e^{|t|^{C}}$ there, and $|f(a+it)|\ll(1+|t|)^{\alpha}$, $|f(b+it)|\ll(1+|t|)^{\beta}$, then
$$|f(\sigma+it)|\ll(1+|t|)^{\ell(\sigma)},\qquad \ell(\sigma)=\alpha\,\frac{b-\sigma}{b-a}+\beta\,\frac{\sigma-a}{b-a},$$
for $a\le\sigma\le b$. Applying this on every strip shows that $\mu$ is convex: its graph lies below each chord. (Apply it to $(s-1)\zeta(s)$, which is entire; the factor $s-1$ adds $1$ to the exponent on both edges and therefore to $\ell$, and is then removed.) A convex function that vanishes on $[1,\infty)$ cannot increase anywhere, otherwise it would tend to $+\infty$ to the right; so $\mu$ is non-increasing, and a finite convex function is continuous.

Now take $\delta>0$ and the strip $-\delta\le\sigma\le1+\delta$. On the right edge $|\zeta|\le\zeta(1+\delta)$, exponent $\beta=0$. On the left edge $|\zeta(-\delta+it)|=|\chi(-\delta+it)|\,|\zeta(1+\delta-it)|\ll|t|^{1/2+\delta}$, exponent $\alpha=\tfrac12+\delta$. At $\sigma=\tfrac12$,
$$\ell(\tfrac12)=\Bigl(\tfrac12+\delta\Bigr)\frac{(1+\delta)-\tfrac12}{1+2\delta}=\frac{(\tfrac12+\delta)^2}{1+2\delta}=\frac14+\frac\delta2.$$
Taking $\delta=2\varepsilon$ gives $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll|t|^{1/4+\varepsilon}$. The same interpolation between $\mu(0)=\tfrac12$ and $\mu(1)=0$ gives $\mu(\sigma)\le\frac{1-\sigma}{2}$ on $[0,1]$.

blocks.title: Why 1/4 is the trivial bound and LH is cancellation
blocks.body:
The convexity bound has a transparent meaning. The Riemann–Siegel form of the approximate functional equation says that for large $t$, with $N=\lfloor\sqrt{t/2\pi}\rfloor$,
$$\zeta(\tfrac12+it)=\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2-it}+\chi(\tfrac12+it)\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2+it}+O(t^{-1/4}).$$
Both sums have length about $\sqrt t$, and $|\chi(\tfrac12+it)|=1$. Bounding every term by its absolute value gives at most $2\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2}<4\sqrt N\approx4(t/2\pi)^{1/4}$ (Example 1). So convexity is what you get by assuming no cancellation at all among the phases $t\log n$.

If the terms $n^{-it}$ behaved like independent random unit vectors, a sum of $M$ of them would typically have size about $\sqrt M$. A bound of the form $\bigl|\sum_{n\le M}n^{-it}\bigr|\ll M^{1/2}t^{\varepsilon}$ for all $M\le\sqrt t$ would, after partial summation, give LH. Thus LH is a square-root cancellation statement for the exponential sums $\sum n^{-it}=\sum e^{-it\log n}$, and the attack on it is the theory of [[exponential-sums|exponential sums]]: Weyl differencing and van der Corput's method replace the sum by sums with smoother phases, and each step saves a power of $t$.

blocks.title: History of the exponent
blocks.body:
Writing $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll|t|^{c+\varepsilon}$:
- $c=\tfrac14=0.25$: convexity.
- $c=\tfrac16\approx0.1667$: Hardy and Littlewood, using Weyl's differencing method (around 1920). The exponent $\tfrac16$ is often called the Weyl exponent, and Weyl-strength bounds are a benchmark for every $L$-function.
- $c=\tfrac{9}{56}\approx0.1607$: Bombieri and Iwaniec (1986), a new method for exponential sums.
- $c=\tfrac{32}{205}\approx0.1561$: Huxley (2005), refining Bombieri–Iwaniec.
- $c=\tfrac{13}{84}\approx0.1548$: Bourgain (2017), combining the Bombieri–Iwaniec method with decoupling estimates from harmonic analysis.

Many intermediate improvements, by van der Corput, Titchmarsh, Kolesnik and others, are omitted. The progress since 1920 is less than $0.012$ in the exponent, which gives a sense of how hard the problem is.

blocks.title: Equivalent forms and consequences
blocks.body:
1. (Hardy and Littlewood) LH holds if and only if for every integer $k\ge1$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, $\displaystyle\int_0^T|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^{2k}dt\ll T^{1+\varepsilon}$.
2. (Backlund) LH holds if and only if for every $\sigma>\tfrac12$ the number of zeros with $\beta\ge\sigma$ and $T\le\gamma\le T+1$ is $o(\log T)$. For comparison, the total number of zeros with $T\le\gamma\le T+1$ is $O(\log T)$, and about $\frac{1}{2\pi}\log T$ on average.
3. (Littlewood) The Riemann hypothesis implies LH, and in fact gives $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll\exp\bigl(C\log t/\log\log t\bigr)$ for some constant $C$.
4. (Ingham) If $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll t^{c}$, then $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{(2+4c)(1-\sigma)}(\log T)^5$. In particular LH implies the density hypothesis of [[zero-density]], and hence $p_{n+1}-p_n\ll p_n^{1/2+\varepsilon}$.

blocks.title: Subconvexity for other L-functions
blocks.body:
Every $L$-function with a functional equation has a convexity bound obtained exactly as above. For a Dirichlet $L$-function with primitive character $\chi$ modulo $q$, the functional equation relates $L(s,\chi)$ to $L(1-s,\bar\chi)$ with a factor of size about $(q(|t|+1))^{1/2-\sigma}$, and Phragmén–Lindelöf gives $L(\tfrac12,\chi)\ll_\varepsilon q^{1/4+\varepsilon}$. A subconvexity bound is any bound $q^{1/4-\delta}$ with fixed $\delta>0$. Known landmarks:
- Burgess (1962–63): $L(\tfrac12,\chi)\ll_\varepsilon q^{3/16+\varepsilon}$, from his bound for short character sums.
- Conrey and Iwaniec (2000): $q^{1/6+\varepsilon}$ for quadratic characters, the Weyl exponent in the $q$-aspect.
- Michel and Venkatesh (2010): subconvexity for all $\mathrm{GL}(2)$ $L$-functions, in every aspect at once.

Subconvexity is often exactly what an application needs: a power saving over the trivial bound, however small. Several equidistribution theorems (for example of lattice points on spheres or of special points on modular curves) are proved by reducing them to subconvex bounds for suitable $L$-values.

blocks.title: Example 1: the trivial bound for the approximate functional equation
blocks.body:
Prove that for every integer $N\ge2$
$$2\sqrt{N+1}-2<\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac1{\sqrt n}<2\sqrt N-1,$$
and deduce that the two main sums in the approximate functional equation have total absolute value less than $4(t/2\pi)^{1/4}$.
blocks.solution:
For $n\ge1$,
$$\sqrt{n+1}-\sqrt n=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}+\sqrt n}<\frac1{2\sqrt n}<\frac{1}{\sqrt n+\sqrt{n-1}}=\sqrt n-\sqrt{n-1}.$$
Summing the left inequality over $1\le n\le N$ telescopes to $\sqrt{N+1}-1<\tfrac12\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2}$. Summing the right inequality over $2\le n\le N$ gives $\tfrac12\sum_{2\le n\le N}n^{-1/2}<\sqrt N-1$, so $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2}<1+2\sqrt N-2=2\sqrt N-1$.

With $N=\lfloor\sqrt{t/2\pi}\rfloor$ each main sum is at most $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1/2}<2\sqrt N\le2(t/2\pi)^{1/4}$, and $|\chi(\tfrac12+it)|=1$, so together they are less than $4(t/2\pi)^{1/4}$. For $N=10$ the sum is $5.021$, between $4.633$ and $5.325$; for $N=100$ it is $18.590$, between $18.100$ and $19$.

blocks.title: Example 2: LH pins down the whole function μ
blocks.body: Show that LH is equivalent to $\mu(\sigma)=\max(0,\tfrac12-\sigma)$ for all real $\sigma$. You may use that $\mu(\sigma)\ge0$ for $\sigma\ge\tfrac12$, which follows from mean values: $\frac1T\int_1^T|\zeta(\sigma+it)|^2dt$ tends to $\zeta(2\sigma)$ for $\sigma>\tfrac12$ and grows like $\log T$ for $\sigma=\tfrac12$, which would be impossible if $|\zeta(\sigma+it)|\ll|t|^{-a}$ with $a>0$.
blocks.solution:
If $\mu(\sigma)=\max(0,\tfrac12-\sigma)$ everywhere then $\mu(\tfrac12)=0$, which is LH.

Conversely assume $\mu(\tfrac12)=0$. For $\sigma\ge\tfrac12$, since $\mu$ is non-increasing and $\mu\ge0$ there, $0\le\mu(\sigma)\le\mu(\tfrac12)=0$. For $\sigma<\tfrac12$ we have $1-\sigma>\tfrac12$, so $\mu(1-\sigma)=0$ and the relation $\mu(\sigma)=\tfrac12-\sigma+\mu(1-\sigma)$ gives $\mu(\sigma)=\tfrac12-\sigma$.

So under LH the graph of $\mu$ is the broken line made of $\tfrac12-\sigma$ on the left and $0$ on the right, meeting at the critical line, while convexity only guarantees the chord from $(0,\tfrac12)$ to $(1,0)$ as an upper bound. The convexity bound is the straight line; LH is the corner.

blocks.title: Example 3: numbers at modest height
blocks.body: At $t=1000$ compare $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)$ with the two main sums of the approximate functional equation ($N=12$). Then look at the size of $|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|$ for $t\le1000$ and compare it with $t^{1/4}$.
blocks.solution:
Numerically, $|\zeta(\tfrac12+1000i)|\approx0.998$, and the main sums with $N=12$ reproduce it with an error of about $0.114$, compared with $t^{-1/4}\approx0.178$. At $t=10^4$ ($N=39$) the error is about $0.111$ against $t^{-1/4}=0.1$. So the error really is of order $t^{-1/4}$ and the approximation is excellent.

On the other hand $|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|$ exceeds $9.4$ near $t\approx897.85$, while $897.85^{1/4}\approx5.47$. This does not contradict anything: $\ll$ hides constants, and at such heights $\log t$ factors are as large as small powers of $t$. The Lindelöf hypothesis and its relatives are statements about growth rates and cannot be tested by looking at values at moderate height.

blocks.title: Example 4: from bounds on ζ to density exponents and prime gaps
blocks.body: Using item 4 of the theorem on equivalent forms together with the theorem on primes in short intervals from [[zero-density]] (density exponent $A$ gives intervals $x^{\theta}$ for every $\theta>1-1/A$), compute $A$ and $\theta$ for $c=\tfrac14,\ \tfrac16,\ \tfrac{13}{84}$ and for LH ($c\to0$).
blocks.solution:
Ingham's bound has $A=2+4c$.
- $c=\tfrac14$: $A=3$, $\theta>\tfrac23$.
- $c=\tfrac16$: $A=\tfrac83$, $\theta>1-\tfrac38=\tfrac58$. This is Ingham's 1937 theorem $p_{n+1}-p_n\ll p_n^{5/8+\varepsilon}$.
- $c=\tfrac{13}{84}$: $A=2+\tfrac{52}{84}=\tfrac{55}{21}$, $\theta>1-\tfrac{21}{55}=\tfrac{34}{55}\approx0.618$.
- LH: $A=2+\varepsilon$, every $\theta>\tfrac12$.

Note that Huxley's density exponent $\tfrac{12}{5}=2.4$ is better than $\tfrac{55}{21}\approx2.619$: density estimates improve not only through bounds for $\zeta$ but also through better large values estimates for Dirichlet polynomials.

blocks.body:
- LH is not RH. It is a statement about size; it is compatible with zeros off the critical line, provided they are sparse in the sense of Backlund's criterion.
- $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)$ is unbounded. LH asserts growth slower than every power of $t$, not boundedness.
- The exponents in the history list are infima: a bound $\ll t^{13/84+\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon$ is what is proved, not $\ll t^{13/84}$.
- Convexity needs a functional equation and polynomial growth on the edges. An arbitrary Dirichlet series has no such bound for free.
- Numerical values at moderate height say nothing about these exponents (Example 3).

The convexity bound is a direct consequence of the [[functional-equation]], and all subconvexity results for $\zeta$ come from estimates for [[exponential-sums]]. LH is equivalent to bounds for all [[moments]] of $\zeta$, implies the density hypothesis ([[zero-density]]) and so gives good results on primes in short intervals ([[prime-patterns]]). It is itself a consequence of the [[rh|Riemann hypothesis]], and the [[grh|generalized Riemann hypothesis]] likewise implies a generalized Lindelöf hypothesis for [[l-functions]], whose subconvexity problem is a central theme of modern analytic number theory.

1. Use the functional equation to show that $\mu(-1)=\tfrac32$ and more generally $\mu(\sigma)=\tfrac12-\sigma$ for $\sigma\le0$.
2. Show that LH implies $\int_0^T|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^{2k}dt\ll_{k,\varepsilon}T^{1+\varepsilon}$ for every $k$ (the easy direction of the Hardy–Littlewood equivalence).
3. Assuming the approximate functional equation, show that a bound $\bigl|\sum_{n\le M}n^{-it}\bigr|\ll M^{1/2}t^{\varepsilon}$ for all $M\le\sqrt{t/2\pi}$ would imply $\zeta(\tfrac12+it)\ll t^{2\varepsilon}$. (Use partial summation.)
4. Show that $\chi(s)\chi(1-s)=1$ and deduce that $|\chi(\tfrac12+it)|=1$ for real $t$.
